To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a syntactic characterization exists for the class of concepts classifiable according to a classification in the limit paradigm with a mind change bound, and (2) this syntactic characterization is related to the difference hiearchy over the class of possible data of the classification paradigm.
the class of concepts classifiable in the limit according to some criteria is characterized by a syntactic representation that can be defined from the class itself.

the class of concepts classifiable in the limit with a given mind change bound is exactly the class of concepts whose syntactic representation is contained in a particular difference hierarchy over some topological space.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how much syntactic structure is required to perform a given classification task.
the following question: what is the minimal syntactic representation of concepts that is sufficient to guarantee learnability in some classification paradigm?
the question of what it means to learn a class of concepts in a particular paradigm, and we provide a syntactic characterization of what it means.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the syntactic characterization is a syntactic characterization of the difference hierarchy of the topological space associated with a learning paradigm.
the difference hierarchy over a topological space can be seen as the canonical syntactic representation for a class of concepts that is classifiable according to some classification paradigm.
the class of concepts learnable in the limit with an ordinal mind change bound by a computable classifier is precisely the class of concepts definable in the corresponding difference hierarchy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide a syntactic characterization of classification with a mind change bound in terms of a topological space that is naturally defined from a given learning paradigm.

the syntactic characterization of the class of classifiable concepts in a logical setting with ordinal mind change bound is given by the difference hierarchy of the topological space defined from the class.
the difference hierarchy over a topological space is a natural syntactic framework to represent classes of concepts that are learnable with a mind change bound.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a learning paradigm is well-behaved if it can be represented by a difference hierarchy.

syntactic characterizations of learnability can be obtained for classification paradigms in which no syntactic representation is imposed on the class of underlying concepts to be learned, but rather on the class of possible observations of the learning paradigm.
the syntactic characterization of a classification paradigm is a powerful tool for proving that a given paradigm is learnable.
